proposals.impact: restore daily content output blocked since 05:48 this morning
proposals.observation: Two CI workflows failed in the last 24 hours: "Funnel-Hack Digest" at 10:05 and "Daily Blog Post" at 05:48. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published. With zero quiz sessions in the 48-hour window, organic search traffic from daily posts is the only active top-of-funnel mechanism. A failed blog workflow means no new post published today, no new indexed page, and the queue drains to zero by tomorrow.
proposals.proposal: Inspect the Daily Blog Post workflow logs, identify the failure reason (most likely a missing env var given the pattern of the three MailerLite-related redeploys today), and patch the workflow or its env configuration so tonight's scheduled run fires. This is a single file edit to the workflow YAML or its associated secret reference. Because .github/workflows/* is blocked for direct Fred edits, Joel must apply this manually, but the diagnosis is: check whether the workflow references a MAILERLITE_API_TOKEN or OPENAI_API_KEY that was scoped to functions but not to Actions secrets. Compare the working MailerLite redeploy commits (686a23e, 801e4c7) against the workflow's env block.

proposals.impact: capitalise on 66.67% open rate by tightening the first CTA to convert readers already engaged
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has the highest open rate of the three sequences at 66.67% (8 of 12 opens). That is a warm, attentive audience. High open rates without a corresponding data point for clicks or replies suggest the email is being read but not acted on. The ICP for this script — the person who watches every penny but still does not build — responds to precision and acknowledgement of their specific anxiety, not general encouragement. If the first CTA in that sequence is soft or generic, these readers will finish the email, feel seen, and close the tab.
proposals.proposal: Replace the existing CTA paragraph in the Money Vigilance sequence's first email. The current text (captured below) uses a generic invitation. The replacement grounds the ask in a concrete, specific scenario that only Joel could write — the kind of moment a Money Vigilance person actually lives through — and makes the next step feel proportionate rather than large.
proposals.current_text: If this sounds familiar, I'd love to help you explore what's really going on with your money. Book a free clarity call and let's see if we're a good fit.
proposals.new_text: If you recognise that feeling — the spreadsheet is immaculate, the ISA is funded, and you still lie awake running the numbers — then the work underneath is not more tracking. It is working out what the tracking is protecting you from. If you want to look at that honestly, my introductory session gives us 90 minutes to do exactly that. The link is below.

proposals.impact: bridge the gap between 52.63% opens and actual coaching enquiries by adding a specific story beat
proposals.observation: The Money Avoidance automation has 19 sends and a 52.63% open rate — solid reach, but the sequence name and ICP suggest these are people who already know they avoid their finances and feel some shame about it. A reader who opens an email called "Money Avoidance" is already doing something courageous. If email 2 in that sequence does not meet that courage with something equally specific and grounded, the reader's avoidance pattern reasserts and they do not click. With the quiz at zero sessions, this automation is one of the only active conversion paths right now.
proposals.proposal: Add a short, specific story paragraph to the Money Avoidance sequence's second email, before the existing CTA. The paragraph references a real texture of avoidance — not a metaphor, not a framework, a described moment — so the reader feels accurately seen rather than categorised. This increases the probability they take the next step because the email has demonstrated Joel understands the interior of their situation, not just its label.
proposals.current_text: Money avoidance doesn't mean you don't care about money. It usually means you care so much that looking at it feels too risky. Here's what we can do about it.
proposals.new_text: Money avoidance does not mean you do not care about money. It usually means you care so much that looking at it feels too risky. There is a version of this that is very quiet. The bank app is on the second screen of the folder. The tax return tab has been open in the browser for six weeks. You know roughly what the numbers say. Roughly is doing a lot of work there. That gap between roughly and actually is where most of the anxiety lives, and it is smaller than it feels. If you want to close it without it becoming a production, that is what the introductory session is for.
